entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13231"/><div sID="gen25005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13231"/>5-9. He describes the promises, and also the conditions of the covenant; Levi's observance of the conditions and reward (compare <reference osisRef="Num.25.11-Num.25.13">Nu 25:11-13</reference>, Phinehas' zeal); and on the other hand the violation of the conditions, and consequent punishment of the present priests. "Life" here includes the perpetuity implied in <reference osisRef="Num.25.13">Nu 25:13</reference>, "everlasting priesthood." "Peace" is specified both here and there. Maurer thus explains it; the Hebrew is, literally, "My covenant was with him, life and peace (to be given him on My part), and I gave them to him: (and on his part) fear (that is, reverence), and he did fear Me," &c. The former portion of the verse expresses the promise, and Jehovah's fulfilment of it; the latter, the condition, and Levi's steadfastness to it (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.8">De 33:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">9</reference>). The Jewish priests self-deceivingly claimed the privileges of the covenant, while neglecting the conditions of it, as if God were bound by it to bless them, while they were free from all the obligation which it imposed to serve Him. The covenant is said to be not merely "of life and peace," but "life and peace"; for the keeping of God's law is its own reward (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.11">Psa 19:11</reference>). <div eID="gen25005" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13236"/><div sID="gen25021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13236"/>10-16. Reproof of those who contracted marriages with foreigners and repudiated their Jewish wives. <div eID="gen25021" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13237"/><div sID="gen25022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13237"/><hi type="bold">10. Have we not all one father?--</hi>Why, seeing we all have one common origin, "do we deal treacherously against one another" ("His brother" being a general expression implying that all are "brethren" and sisters as children of the same Father above (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.3-1Thess.4.6">1Th 4:3-6</reference>), and so including the wives so injured)? namely, by putting away our Jewish wives, and taking foreign women to wife (compare Mal 2:14 and Mal 2:11; <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.1-Ezra.9.9">Ezr 9:1-9</reference>), and so violating "the covenant" made by Jehovah with "our fathers," by which it was ordained that we should be a people separated from the other peoples of the world (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.24">Le 20:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.3">De 7:3</reference>). To intermarry with the heathen would defeat this purpose of Jehovah, who was the common Father of the Israelites in a peculiar sense in which He was not Father of the heathen. The "one Father" is Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Job.31.15">Job 31:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.6">1Co 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.6">Ep 4:6</reference>). "Created us": not merely physical creation, but "created us" to be His peculiar and chosen people (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.18">Psa 102:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Is 43:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">45:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">60:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>), [Calvin]. How marked the contrast between the honor here done to the female sex, and the degradation to which Oriental women are generally subjected! <div eID="gen25022" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13244"/><div sID="gen25038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13244"/><hi type="bold">17. wearied ... Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.43.24">Is 43:24</reference>). This verse forms the transition to Mal 3:1, &c. The Jewish skeptics of that day said virtually, God delighteth in evil-doers (inferring this from the prosperity of the surrounding heathen, while they, the Jews, were comparatively not prosperous: forgetting that their attendance to minor and external duties did not make up for their neglect of the weightier duties of the law; for example, the duty they owed their wives, just previously discussed); or (if not) Where (is the proof that He is) the God of judgment? To this the reply (Mal 3:1) is, "The Lord whom ye seek, and whom as messenger of the covenant (that is, divine ratifier of God's covenant with Israel) ye delight in (thinking He will restore Israel to its proper place as first of the nations), shall suddenly come," not as a Restorer of Israel temporally, but as a consuming Judge against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference>, 19, 20). The "suddenly" implies the unpreparedness of the Jews, who, to the last of the siege, were expecting a temporal deliverer, whereas a destructive judgment was about to destroy them. So skepticism shall be rife before Christ's second coming. He shall suddenly and unexpectedly come then also as a consuming Judge to unbelievers (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3">2Pe 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">4</reference>). Then, too, they shall affect to seek His coming, while really denying it (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Is 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.15">Jr 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">Eze 12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.27">27</reference>). <chapter eID="Mal.2"/>
